extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature/aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Short, discursive essays arguing aesthetic and cultural criteria for valuing various forms of art, popular literature, and social symbols (pastoral, heraldry, 'useful information', ugliness, farce). Intended as rhetoric to reshape tastes rather than prescriptive how-to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetizing of natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should realize scientific or natural facts poetically — transforming ordinary observations (e.g., 'the sky was blue and the grass green') into symbolic, imaginative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts an early habit where discovery of a natural fact 'was immediately followed by the realization of it as a fact of poetry' with the modern tendency to ignore scientific portent. Examples and counterfactuals are used (e.g., 'planetary patriotism', wearing one's star's heraldry). Anti-pattern: treating scientific facts as mere weather-notes and failing to let fancy 'play with the planets.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as retrospective realization
rubrics_metrics.description: The prime function of imagination is to make settled things strange and to view past and present eras through the appropriate 'eyes' (e.g., seeing Delphi as a Greek, Jerusalem as a Crusader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination 'calls the dead out of their graves' and turns truisms into paradoxes; it should not merely invent new republics but re-enchant what exists. Anti-pattern: imagination used only for novelty rather than for re-visioning the familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the Arcadian/pastoral ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal shepherd and pastoral imagery preserved a conception of 'a dignity in simplicity and a dignity in labour' that served as a moral/cultural counterbalance to aristocratic triumphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if old pastoral art is sentimentally tawdry, its residual value lies in presenting an 'Ideal Shepherd' that makes the drudgery of life 'worth while as a whole.' Practical implication: retaining or reviving idealized images (even if not literally true) benefits social imagination. Anti-pattern: discarding all idealizing images as merely false or childish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideals/background images should exist for ordinary trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should cultivate heroic or ideal images for commonplace trades (postman, grocer, plumber) analogous to the Ideal Shepherd so that ordinary drudgery is given meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes symbolic patronage (e.g., 'Patron Saint of Plumbers') and argues that such ideals force craftsmen to believe in a higher exemplum. Anti-pattern: democratic rhetoric that merely levels down aristocratic grandeur ('The Duke is no better than you') rather than extending magnificence to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and social function of 'useless' information and news
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular taste for trivial 'information for information's sake' (odd facts, curiosities) is not mere vulgarity but an expression of a youthful, inquisitive stage of a people — a 'taste for news' that treats the world as a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that readers of trivial magazines are 'as disinterested as a prophet' and that the appetite for odd facts is a social virtue linked to enthusiasm and entering history. Suggests bridging science and popular news to rebuild a link between discovery and communal imagination. Anti-pattern: treating interest in trivial facts as purely senile or morally degrading without recognizing its social/psychological roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial symbols and heraldry educate aesthetic sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial signs (heraldry, shop signs) carry a pictorial/poetic quality that influences hearts without passing through intellect, contributing to aesthetic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues letters and signs were originally pictorial; symbols like the red lion are not mere convenience but carriers of feeling. Recommends restoring symbolic pageantry to democracy so common citizens can share the 'human magnificence' once reserved for aristocracy. Anti-pattern: reducing all symbolic imagery to mere utility or ridiculing public ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires pageantry and symbolic exuberance
rubrics_metrics.description: For democratic society to cherish its mission, it must develop its own heraldry, colours, and public festivities rather than mock or erase traditional splendour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: French revolutionary festivals attempted new religions and symbols; English democracy erred by decreasing past magnificence rather than enlarging it. Practical stance: encourage civic pageantry and acceptance of occasional 'making fools of ourselves' to allow democracy to 'blossom.' Anti-pattern: modern prudishness or Puritanical seriousness that laughs at ornament and colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject narrow classical standard of beauty; value ugliness and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek ideal imposed a narrow aesthetic asceticism; true aesthetic appreciation recognizes 'ugliness' as expressive vitality — individuality and forcefulness in face or form are beautiful in their own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Chinese, Japanese, and medieval art (gargoyles, Rembrandt) as traditions that celebrate goggle eyes, sprawling claws, strong noses. Principle: 'one star differeth from another in glory' — variety should be prized. Anti-pattern: judging all faces or forms against a single classical prototype (Venus of Milo) and labeling divergence 'ugly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque as expression of vitality, not mere comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: What critics call the 'grotesque' often signals dramatic expressiveness and fierce vitality rather than comic mockery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes grotesque ornament (e.g., dragons, gargoyles) as intended to convey energy and bold departure, comparable to crags and pines in nature. Anti-pattern: dismissing grotesque elements as merely laughable or inferior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and defend lighter/wilder art forms (farce, pantomime, detective stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce, pantomime, detective stories and other 'lighter' arts are legitimate artistic sensations and should not be treated as inherently debased; contempt leads to neglect and poor quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that labeling such forms as 'degenerate' causes them to be 'neglected children' whose eventual quality suffers; if all forms were equally scorned, any genre could become 'despicable' — the fault lies in the attitude. Practical implication: treat lighter forms with the same seriousness of cultivation as 'high' forms. Anti-pattern: automatic hierarchical condemnation of popular genres.
